question.text: A calorimeter of negligible heat capacity contains <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></math> water at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>40</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>. The water cools to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>35</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C </mi></math>in <math><mn>5 </mn><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></math>. If water is now replaced by a liquid of the same volume as that of water at the same initial temperature it cools to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>35</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math> in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></math>. Given specific heats of water and liquid are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4200</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2100</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> respectively. Find the density of liquid give the answer in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>kg</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></math>. [Assume Newton law of cooling is applicable]
